checkpoints: A correctly-working debounce only limits the COUNT of requests fired within a single typing burst — it says nothing about response ORDERING; these are two independent axes debounce never touches.

Concrete counter-example: type "admin", pause long enough → request A departs; then keep typing "zora42", pause again → request B also departs — two separate, fully legitimate requests despite debounce working exactly as designed.

Because network latency is variable, nothing guarantees A returns before B: if the OLDER request A is delayed and lands AFTER the NEWER request B, A's callback runs last and overwrites already-correct state with a stale verdict.

First shield, core mechanic: give each fetch its own AbortController, and in the effect cleanup call controller.abort() (alongside clearTimeout) the instant the value changes, so the previous in-flight request is cancelled.

First shield, completeness detail: the cancelled request's rejection (AbortError) must be caught and deliberately ignored, and checking !controller.signal.aborted immediately before committing covers a response that lands just as the abort takes effect.

Second shield, stale guard: attach an identifier (the username itself, or an incrementing request-id) to each query and only commit its result when that identifier still matches the field's CURRENT value — this is the required fallback when the transport cannot cleanly cancel (no abort support, or a server-side queue that keeps processing regardless of client abort).

The unifying invariant both shields enforce: only the response whose identifier/non-aborted status matches the field's CURRENT value may ever be written to state — not simply whichever request happened to be sent last.

Senior nuance: React Strict Mode double-invokes every effect in dev (mount → cleanup → mount), so cleanup must cancel BOTH the timer AND the controller, or a single keystroke can double-fire the request.
Gate scope must match user progress: parsing the whole schema right at Next fails on every step that hasn't been touched yet, so the wizard deadlocks at step 1 and can never pass.
Next instead runs methods.trigger(['account.email', 'account.password']) — the same resolver, scoped to exactly that field subset.
trigger returns a boolean: await → early return on failure → setStep only after passing — validate first, advance second.
trigger also populates formState.errors so FieldError renders — decision and display in one call, its dual role.
Each step's green light does NOT make the final parse redundant, because each sub-schema only sees its own slice of data.

A contradiction SPANNING multiple steps (a root-level .refine over the combined object, e.g. a rule tying age to a preferences choice) stays invisible until the whole payload is parsed at once — which is exactly what handleSubmit does with the root wizardSchema before the single POST, the only place that can catch this class of cross-step error.
If that final parse fails, onInvalid (handleSubmit's second callback) jumps the user back to the FIRST step still carrying an error.
A viable variant: split sub-schema safeParse (or .pick) for the decision and trigger for rendering — same result, just separating the two responsibilities, at the cost of two calls.
The bug is that the effect never returns a cleanup — it is not a logic bug inside the setTimeout callback.

A real debounce is "every new event resets the clock": in React, that reset IS the effect's cleanup — React runs the PREVIOUS effect's cleanup before running the CURRENT one when a dependency changes.
return () => clearTimeout(handle) is the line that actually cancels the pending timer, so only the final keystroke's timer survives the full 500ms of silence to fire.

In this snippet the effect ends with no return at all, so setTimeout is reduced to a plain delay, not a debounce: typing "zora42" re-runs the effect 6 times, scheduling 6 uncancelled timers that all fire ~500ms after they were each created, so the Network tab shows 6 requests.
The banner flickers because the responses for the intermediate prefixes keep landing one after another (and can arrive out of send order) and keep overwriting availability.
The one-line fix: add return () => clearTimeout(handle) at the end of the effect.

For full race-safety, upgrade to the AbortController variant: create a controller inside the effect, pass controller.signal into fetch, and have the cleanup call both clearTimeout(handle) AND controller.abort() — an aborted response throws AbortError and never touches setAvailability.

To verify: use Playwright pressSequentially("zora42", { delay: 50 }) with a request counter attached via page.on("request", ...), then assert requestCount === 1 and that the final data-state settles on the correct verdict for "zora42".

The root cause is key={index} — React uses key to match elements between two renders to decide whether to REUSE or REMOUNT a node, and an index is NOT an identity, only an entry's current position in the array.

With rows A/B/C, remove(1) deletes entry B from the fields array, which slides C from index 2 down to index 1; on the next render React sees key={1} (previously B) is still key={1} (now C), so it concludes this is the same node and reuses the exact DOM/instance that used to render B.

register/Controller inside that reused node have already been rebound by RHF to items.1.* — i.e. C's data — so the reused DOM and the rebound data are out of sync, which reads on screen as jumped/scrambled values.

This bug only surfaces when removing or moving a row IN THE MIDDLE, because that is exactly when the remaining entries' indices actually change; pure append-at-the-end leaves every existing entry's index unchanged, so an index key stays 'accidentally correct' until a middle removal or reorder happens.

useFieldArray exists precisely to solve this: every entry in fields carries a UUID field.id stable PER ENTRY rather than per position, so key={field.id} lets React match by IDENTITY instead of position, keeping surviving rows' exact DOM and values regardless of which entry is removed or swapped.

These are two different axes: the React key must be identity (field.id), while register/Controller paths (items.${index}.description, items.${index}.quantity) and per-row error lookups (errors.items?.[index]) are correctly positional because RHF actively rebinds those paths after every mutation — index in paths is correct, index as key is the bug.
The fix is to change key={index} to key={field.id}, leaving every use of index in paths/errors untouched.

Verification: build three rows A/B/C, call remove(1), and assert desc-0 still has 'A' while desc-1 now has 'C' (toHaveValue) — the key={index} version fails this deterministically; add a matching assertion after move(1, 0) to cover the reorder case too.
Confirms the single shared useForm instance wired through FormProvider across all three steps is the correct baseline architecture, not a defect to change.

Identifies the highest-severity bug: conditionally rendering only the active step ({step === 0 && <StepAccount/>}) actually unmounts the other steps' DOM nodes, and since these are uncontrolled inputs the typed values live in the DOM itself.
States the concrete symptom of that bug: clicking Back after Next shows the previously typed email/password fields empty — a real data-loss bug, not a cosmetic one.
Gives the correct fix for that bug: always render every step and hide inactive ones with CSS (e.g. display:none) so the DOM nodes — and the values inside them — never unmount.

Identifies the second bug: defaultValues only seeds account.email/account.password, omitting the profile and preferences keys, even though a single shared form instance needs the complete shape from the very first render.

States the concrete consequence and fix: unvisited steps leave profile/preferences undefined in getValues(), which fails the root wizardSchema parse (or lets undefined leak into the POST body) at final submit — fixed by declaring the full WizardInput defaults for all three steps up front.

Identifies the third bug with its fix: Next/Back render as bare <Button onPress> with no type attribute, so inside a <form> they default to type="submit", meaning Enter or a Next click calls handleSubmit prematurely — fixed by type="button" on Next/Back and a real type="submit" only on the last step.
create() runs exactly once at module scope, and the result is a singleton shared by every place that imports it, so no Provider or Context tree is ever needed for a Zustand store.
When a component calls useStore(selector), it registers a subscription whose scope is exactly the value the selector returns, not a generic subscription to 'the state'.
After every set(), Zustand re-runs EACH subscriber's selector and compares the old result against the new one with Object.is — differing means notify and re-render, equal means skip silently.
With a primitive selector like (s) => s.count, the component re-renders exactly when count actually changes.

A selector returning an action, like (s) => s.increment, returns a forever-stable reference because the action is declared once in the initializer, so Object.is is always true and that component NEVER re-renders no matter how many times the state changes.

This is the opposite of Context: when a Context value changes, EVERY consumer in the tree re-renders regardless of which small slice of the value it actually reads, and React.memo at that point only patches each component rather than stopping the signal at the source the way Zustand's selector does.
The trap to remember is that calling the hook with no selector at all is equivalent to subscribing to the whole state object, so any field changing drags along a re-render.
The real lesson isn't 'Zustand is faster than Context' but that the subscribe-by-selector model gives fine-grained control over render scope, a control Context has no built-in mechanism for.
Jotai models state as a dependency graph of atoms rather than one big object, with counterAtom as the primitive source node.
A derived atom, declared atom((get) => ...), has no setter — its value is always COMPUTED from the atoms it reads rather than assigned directly.

Dependency tracking is automatic: every get(counterAtom) call inside the read function is recorded by Jotai as a dependency edge, so Jotai always knows doubleCounterAtom and parityAtom depend on counterAtom without anyone writing manual 'refresh' code.
When counterAtom changes value, Jotai walks exactly the edges originating from it and recomputes precisely the dependent atoms, leaving every other unrelated atom untouched.

After recomputing, Jotai compares the new output with the old one via Object.is — if strictly equal, subscribers are NOT notified at all, so a branch that recomputes to the same value never causes a stray re-render.

This is the core difference from useMemo: useMemo caches inside ONE specific component, so five independent useMemo calls run five separate computations with no sharing and each cache disappears the instant its component unmounts, whereas a derived atom's computation runs ONLY ONCE at the atom level and every component subscribing to it receives that same already-computed value, preserving referential identity so nobody duplicates anybody else's work.
Trap 1: atoms must be declared at module scope, since declaring atom(0) inside a component body spawns a brand-new atom on every render and loses all state.

Trap 2: a derived atom returning a fresh object/array each time defeats Object.is dedupe (always sees it as 'different'), causing redundant re-renders — so derived outputs should stay primitive where possible.
States that clean type-checking and 'works on my machine' prove nothing here because all three defects are runtime failures the compiler cannot catch.

Identifies the largest-blast-radius bug: UserSlice and CartSlice both declare a field named loading, and spreading the slices in creation order lets the later slice's loading silently overwrite the earlier one with no exception.

States the concrete consequence and fix: the user's loading state vanishes unnoticed until a spinner bug is reported, fixed by namespacing the field per domain (userLoading/cartLoading) rather than sharing a generic name.

Identifies the second bug: persist(createCartSlice, { name: 'cart' }) wraps only the single cart-slice creator, but persist middleware must wrap the combined/merged creator to serialize the whole store.

States the concrete consequence and fix: UserSlice is silently never written to or restored from localStorage even though nothing throws, fixed by moving persist to wrap the combined creator so one config covers every slice.

Identifies the third issue: checkout imports a user-state-reading function directly from user-slice.ts instead of going through the shared get, which runs fine today but is an immediate circular-dependency risk the moment user-slice needs to read cart data back.

States the fix for that issue: type the creator as StateCreator<AppState, [], [], CartSlice> so get() resolves to the full merged store, letting checkout read get().user directly with no cross-slice file import.
Both widgets re-render because of HOW each one subscribes to the store, not because the data they display actually changed.
WidgetHeader calls useAppStore() with no selector at all, so it subscribes to the entire state object.
Because there is no selector, WidgetHeader gets a brand-new object reference after every set(), so it re-renders on any store change whatsoever.
StatsWidget's selector returns a freshly created inline object literal ({ count, user }) every time it runs.
Object.is sees that new object as a different reference every run, so StatsWidget re-renders on every store change even when count and user are unchanged.
React.memo is the wrong lever here because Zustand's subscription already decides to re-render the component before props are even computed, so memo never gets a chance to block it.

The fix is per-field primitive selectors for WidgetHeader (e.g. useAppStore((s) => s.theme)) and wrapping StatsWidget's selector in useShallow from zustand/react/shallow so the comparison runs per key instead of by whole-object reference.
Verify with React DevTools 'Highlight updates' or a render counter, confirming unrelated widgets stop re-rendering while a picked field still triggers a re-render when it actually changes.
persist is write-through: every set() serializes the ENTIRE state via JSON.stringify and writes synchronously into localStorage, regardless of which field changed.
This whole-state write fires on every keystroke in the search field, which is what causes the visible UI jank.
With a large catalog, that same whole-state serialization can exceed localStorage's size limit and throw QuotaExceededError, silently breaking persistence for that user.
The product-catalog cache doesn't need to persist at all since it's refetchable from the server.
isFilterPanelOpen is a transient UI flag that's fine to lose on reload.
Only theme and cartItemIds are real user preferences worth persisting; searchQuery belongs in the persisted store even less than the catalog does.
Apply partialize in the persist options to whitelist just theme and cartItemIds, cutting both per-write cost and quota pressure without touching the storage backend.
If a genuinely large payload must still persist, the StateStorage adapter contract (getItem/setItem/removeItem) lets you swap in a bigger backend like IndexedDB without changing the store's own code.
